Roule (Gobius roulei) is a small benthic goby inhabiting shallow coastal waters of the northeastern Atlantic, where it occupies sandy and mixed-substrate habitats. At a stable water temperature of 13.5 °C [T = 13.5 °C], the incubation period for developing embryos lasts approximately 15 days. The onset of first feeding, marking the age at birth, occurs at 15 days [ab = 15 days], a duration that aligns with observations in other small-bodied gobiids under comparable thermal regimes at a temperature of 13.5 °C [T = 13.5 °C]. Upon hatching, the prolarvae emerge as extremely small, yolk-dependent individuals; the wet weight at birth is only 0.00016 grams [Wwb = 0.00016 grams], reflecting the tiny size of the fertilised eggs, which measure roughly 1.5 mm in length and 0.45 mm in width. This minimal initial mass necessitates a rapid onset of active feeding once the yolk is resorbed, placing a premium on the timely availability of suitable microzooplanktonic prey in the immediate environment. Field surveys indicate that first feeding typically commences within a few days following eclosion, as the mouth gape opens and the retinal differentiation necessary for prey detection becomes operational.

Sexual maturation in Gobius roulei occurs at a relatively modest body size compared to many confamilial species. Puberty is attained once individuals reach a total length at puberty of 3.41 cm [Lp = 3.41 cm], a value derived from allometric relationships observed in the congeneric Gobius niger. The corresponding wet weight at puberty is 0.32 grams [Wwp = 0.32 grams], indicating that individuals must more than double their mass from birth to the point of gonadal activation. This pronounced growth phase is accompanied by the gradual differentiation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, culminating in the onset of vitellogenesis in females and spermiation in males. During this period of rapid somatic development, young-of-year individuals occupy shallow nursery grounds where food availability is high, allowing them to sustain the elevated ingestion rates necessary to reach the critical size for reproductive activation within their first year of life.

The species exhibits pronounced sexual size dimorphism, a common trait among gobiids where males typically defend nesting territories. The ultimate total length for females reaches 7 cm [Li = 7 cm], while males may continue growing to an ultimate total length for males of 8.5 cm [Li = 8.5 cm], a 21% increase in maximum length that likely confers an advantage in both inter-male competition for nesting sites and in the guarding of adhesive egg masses. This disparity is mirrored in adult body masses: the ultimate wet weight for females is approximately 3.0 grams [Wwi = approximately 3.0 grams], whereas the ultimate wet weight for males is substantially larger at 5.4 grams [Wwi = 5.4 grams]. The gonadosomatic index (GSI) was 7% [GSI = 7%] when measured at 13.5 °C [T = 13.5 °C]. Males allocate considerable resources to territorial defence and nest preparation, whereas females channel energy primarily into gamete production.

Reproductive effort in Gobius roulei is characterised by a strategy of multiple spawning events within a single breeding season, a pattern typical of many small, iteroparous teleosts. During the protracted spawning period, which spans late spring through early autumn in their native range, females deposit their demersal, adhesive eggs in nests excavated under stones or shells, which are subsequently guarded by the male until eclosion. Available data indicate that females produce multiple clutches per season, with each clutch containing a relatively small number of eggs; this repeated reproductive investment is energetically demanding and is closely tied to the seasonal productivity of the coastal ecosystem. The maximum lifespan recorded in the wild at 13.5 °C [T = 13.5 °C] is approximately 8 years [am = approximately 8 years], a relatively extended longevity for a goby of this size that allows individuals to participate in several breeding seasons over the course of their lives. This lifespan value was documented through mark-recapture studies in stable populations along the Atlantic coast of France.

Comparative life-history data from congeneric gobies provide a useful framework for interpreting the ecological adaptations of Gobius roulei. The species' small body size and relatively extended lifespan suggest a life-history strategy that balances early reproduction with the potential for repeated spawning events across multiple years. Sexual size dimorphism is evident, with females attaining a maximum adult total length of 7 cm [Li = 7 cm] and males a larger 8.5 cm [Li = 8.5 cm]; body mass reflects this dimorphism, with adult females reaching an asymptotic mass of 3.0 grams [Wwi = 3.0 grams] and adult males approaching nearly double that at 5.4 grams [Wwi = 5.4 grams]. Males and females reach sexual maturity at a structural length of 3.41 cm [Lp = 3.41 cm], and the body mass at the onset of sexual maturation is 0.32 grams [Wwp = 0.32 grams], indicating that individuals mature before attaining their ultimate dimensions—a pattern that maximises the likelihood of at least some reproductive success in a variable coastal environment. The gonadosomatic index of 7% [GSI = 7%] was recorded at 13.5 °C [T = 13.5 °C].
